notes.69: 83 sîn ane: 'his grandfather', or more loosely 'his ancestor'.
notes.254: The text calls the horse Buzival; given here as Bucephalus.
notes.306: 306 erblûcte sich: 'grew timid, was cowed'; rendered 'was abashed'.

nodes.text: The priest Lambrecht composed it.
He would gladly make known to us
who Alexander was.
Alexander was a wise man;
very many kingdoms he won;
very many lands he destroyed.
His father was called Philip.
This you may well hear
in the Book of Maccabees.
One had to set him well apart,
for Alexander was a heathen.
Now wicked liars say
that he was the son of a conjurer.
Those who ever say it
lie like base cowards,
or those who ever thought it.
He was of true imperial lineage;
let no worthy man ever believe it.
I can name his father well enough.
His lineage was lordly;
he held power over all Greece.
Philip was the name of his father;
all the land of Macedonia was his.
His grandfather was a good warrior;
his rule extended over all the sea.
He had an excellent might.
Oh, how many battles he fought
against King Xerxes!
With great courage he overcame him.
Philip took himself a wife;
she had a noble person.
I will tell you what her name was:
she was called the beautiful Olympias.
She was Alexander's mother.
The lady had a brother
who was also called Alexander;
he held the land in Persia.
He was a prince of such a kind
that he would not be subject to any king.
Nor would he ever flee from any battle,
however things went for him there.
He was a precious warrior
and [wished] also to exercise rightful lordship.
Now I will tell you of Alexander's birth,
how it came about here.
His mother, Lady Olympias —
at the time when she was delivered of him,
a very great calamity befell her.
The earth quaked everywhere;
the thunder was very great;
oh, how violently the storm poured down!
The sky changed,
and the sun grew dark.
Oh, how poorly I can believe that,
for he broke his neck in two!
I will tell you of Philip's stud:
in it a horse was foaled.
It was a wondrous thing.
swift and fierce,
in its make and in its strength.
Its mouth was shaped like an ass's;
its ears were very long,
the head lean and slender.
Its eyes were all the colour
of a flying eagle's.
Its neck was curly-maned;
I think it was of the lion's kind.
On its croup it had cattle's hair,
on its flanks a leopard's spots.
and it was brought before King Philip.
And when he learned its nature,
he had it named Bucephalus.
That seemed good to them all.
The horse was ordered into a stable,
it was abashed in all its might
and was willing to serve him.
It knelt down there before him;
nor did it ever stir after that.
So knowing was the horse's whole bearing
